implementation_notes: The standard library's sync_channel(bound) is a bounded channel whose send blocks once the buffer is full - or a rendezvous channel at bound 0 - while try_send is the non-blocking shed path; the receiver blocks in recv(). That is the pattern with no third-party dependency, appropriate for thread-based consumers and blocking work. The limitation is deliberate: mpsc has one receiver and Receiver is not Sync, so fan-out needs crossbeam-channel or a dispatcher thread, and ownership means the queue's memory is reclaimed deterministically when both ends drop.
pitfalls: Receiver is single-consumer and not Sync: cloning the receiver does not compile, so a worker pool needs a dispatcher, a Mutex<Receiver>, or crossbeam-channel.
send() returns Err only when the receiver is gone; ignoring it silently drops the item.
Dropping the Receiver discards everything still buffered - a shutdown path that drops rx too early loses accepted work.
std::sync::mpsc::channel() (unbounded) is the tempting default and removes the bound entirely.

variants.name: tokio::sync::mpsc::channel(n) with async consumers
variants.implementation_notes: In async Rust the bound is explicit too: tokio::sync::mpsc::channel(n) gives a bounded queue whose send awaits capacity and thus applies backpressure, while unbounded_channel sends immediately and grows without limit; blocking_send/blocking_recv bridge synchronous code. The Receiver is again not clonable, so worker pools either wrap it in Arc<Mutex<_>> or, more idiomatically, run one dispatcher task that spawns per-item tasks and bounds the downstream with a semaphore. A clean shutdown calls close() and then drains, which the module documentation describes explicitly, so buffered work is not silently discarded.
pitfalls: unbounded_channel() never applies backpressure by design; it is the anti-pattern unless the growth is provably bounded.
tokio::spawn per item removes the queue's bound from the consumer side - a semaphore or a second bounded channel must limit concurrency at the dependency.
Dropping the Receiver discards unread messages; call close() and drain for a clean shutdown.
A blocking call inside an async consumer stalls a runtime worker thread; use spawn_blocking instead.
